short_definition: A balance transfer moves existing credit card debt to another card, usually one offering a low or 0% introductory interest rate for a limited period, often in exchange for a one-time fee.
explanation: For a balance transfer, you apply for a new credit card, or use an existing one, that offers a promotional rate on transferred debt. The new issuer pays off your old card, and you then owe the new issuer. Most charge a transfer fee, usually a percentage of the amount moved. The promotional rate lasts a set number of months, then switches to the standard rate.

With little or no interest, more of each payment goes toward the debt itself, which can shorten the payoff time. It works best with a clear repayment plan, such as the debt avalanche or snowball, that clears the balance before the promotion ends.

The risks include the transfer fee, a high standard rate after the promotion, a credit limit lower than your debt, and losing the promotional rate if you miss a payment. Applying can temporarily lower your credit score, and new purchases on the card may be charged a different rate. Terms vary by issuer and country, so read the card agreement before applying.
example: Example (illustrative numbers): You owe $4,000 on a card charging 24% APR. You move it to a card with 0% for 15 months and a 3% fee, so you now owe $4,120. Paying about $275 a month clears it within the 15 months. On the old card, the same debt would have cost several hundred dollars in interest over that time.
common_mistake: Treating the 0% period as breathing room and not paying enough each month to clear the balance before the promotion ends. Whatever is left then accrues interest at a high standard rate.
title: Balance Transfer
